item.title: An All-van-der-Waals Qubit
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Merged-element transmon built entirely from a NbSe2-hBN-NbSe2 van der Waals heterostructure achieves T1,avg=55 μs, T2E,avg=21 μs, and T2R,avg=1.9 μs.

Grade 0.503 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Semiconductor spin qubits” · Sein Park, Sameia Zaman, Junghyun Kim, Junyoung An, Daniel Rodan-Legrain, Hung-Yu Tsao, Chia-Chin Tsai, Aranya Goswami, Réouven Assouly, William P. Banner, Gabriel D. Cutter, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Terry P. Orlando, Gil-Ho Lee, Kyle Serniak, Max Hays, Jeffrey A. Grover, Philip Kim, Pablo Jarillo-Herrero, Joel Î-j. Wang, William D. Oliver

Figure

Energy relaxation and dephasing measurements showing decay traces with representative T1=78±3 μs and distributions averaging T1,avg=55 μs.

Asks

Can an all-van-der-Waals Josephson heterostructure yield a superconducting transmon with coherence times competitive with conventional Al-AlOx-Al circuits in a compact lumped footprint?

But

Ratio EJ/EC≈33, making Ramsey coherence sensitive to quasiparticle-induced charge-parity switching and offset-charge drift.

Tools

NbSe₂-hBN-NbSe₂ heterostructure · cryogenic polymer dry-transfer assembly · circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) · two-tone microwave spectroscopy

Abstract

Advances in solid-state physics, materials science, and device engineering have accelerated the development of superconducting qubits. Among emerging platforms, van der Waals (vdW) materials and their heterostructures are potentially attractive building blocks for quantum devices, yet their realization in qubit architectures remains largely underexplored. Here we report an all-vdW superconducting qubit based on a NbSe₂-hBN-NbSe₂ junction, in which a thin hBN layer simultaneously provides Josephson coupling and capacitive shunting between two NbSe₂ islands, forming a "merged-element" transmon. Temporal characterization using circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) techniques yields an average energy-relaxation time T_(1,avg) = 55 ~μs, Hahn-echo coherence time T_(2E,avg) = 21 ~μs, and Ramsey coherence time T_(2R,avg) = 1.9~μs. The relatively low Ramsey time is primarily attributable to an enhanced sensitivity to charge noise consistent with the realized device parameters and not a fundamental limitation. These results show that lumped-element superconducting qubits based on vdW heterostructures can achieve coherence times comparable to those of conventional Al-AlOx-Al qubits, while offering a reduced device footprint and suppressed stray capacitive coupling.

item.title: Parametric two-qubit gates via Landau-Zener interference
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Parametric two-qubit gates enabled by consecutive Landau-Zener transitions achieve population swap fidelity F≈0.98 on transmons with drive frequency tunable over a continuous window from 10 MHz to 100 MHz.

Grade 0.480 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Charge-insensitive qubit design derived from the Cooper pair box” · Simon Geisert, Albert Hertel, Soeren Ihssen, Zhongyi Jiang, Paul Kugler, Nicolas Zapata, Nicolas Gosling, Ameya Nambisan, Yuan Gao, Asier Galicia, Jéferson R. Guimarães, Yorgo Haddad, Marc Neis, Harsh Bhardwaj, Dmitriy A. Volkov, Juan Cereijo, Marcello Guardascione, Yebin Liu, Markus Jerger, Pavel Bushev, Frank Wilhelm-Mauch, Wolfgang Wernsdorfer, Shai Machnes, Mohammad Ansari, Rami Barends, Ioan M. Pop

Figure

Population swap benchmarking on monolithic transmons showing population transfer vs drive amplitude and time, gate calibration across drive frequencies from 10 MHz to 100 MHz, and exponential fidelity decay fits giving F≈0.98 consistent with T2eff=2±0.5 μs.

Asks

Can quantum interference between consecutive Landau-Zener crossings of a tunable coupler enable fast parametric two-qubit gates at arbitrary drive frequencies?

But

Swap fidelity F≈0.98 is limited by decoherence (T2echo=2.2 μs). Simplified model truncates Hilbert space to three-qubit computational subspace.

Tools

Landau-Zener interferometry · capacitively coupled generalized flux qubits in modular chiplet architecture · monolithic transmon architecture · fast-flux coupler modulation

Abstract

We propose and demonstrate gates between two superconducting qubits based on quantum interference of consecutive Landau-Zener (LZ) transitions. This gate mechanism bridges between baseband and parametric two-qubit control, enabling in situ tuning of the control frequency across a continuous interval up to hundreds of MHz. Another advantage compared to dispersive couplers is that the speed of the LZ gate is on the order of the full coupling strength. We experimentally demonstrate the gate on two platforms, a modular chiplet architecture of coupled generalized flux qubits, and on a monolithic transmon architecture. The combination of tunability and gate speed establishes the LZ gate as a unique tool for multiplexing control pulses and interconnecting superconducting chiplet architectures.

item.title: Engineering dissipation and control pulses for high-fidelity fault-tolerance quantum computing
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Two-photon dissipative confinement autonomously restores dephasing-induced leakage back to the logical cat-state subspace with restoration rate ΓR,1≈4κ2|α|2, yielding final population P−(tf)≈99.64% at tf=0.5/κa under pure dephasing κaϕ=κa.

Grade 0.467 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Charge-insensitive qubit design derived from the Cooper pair box” · Shao-Wei Xu, Zhe-Yuan Zhang, Yi-Tong Shi, Ye-Hong Chen, Yan Xia

Figure

Final target population P−(tf) (red curve) and time-averaged subspace leakage PLeak(Avg) (light-blue curve) plotted against total evolution time tf∈(0,1/κa] in the presence of pure dephasing.

Asks

How to design fast, high-fidelity state transfer protocols for dissipative cat-state qubits that are robust against systematic drive errors and suppress dephasing-induced leakage?

But

Numerical simulation only. Requires drive amplitude εd(t)≪2κ2|α|2 and operation within the bounded time window 12κ2|α|3≪tf≪1κa|α|2.

Tools

shortcut-to-adiabaticity (STA) via inverse engineering · two-photon dissipative confinement · Lindblad master equation simulations · effective two-level subspace mapping

Abstract

Cat-state qubits, a prominent class of bosonic encodings, offer a promising pathway toward hardware-efficient fault-tolerant quantum computing. In this manuscript, we propose an optimally robust control protocol for the cat-state qubits which are stabilized by engineering two-photon dissipation. By deriving an effective two-level description in the cat-state subspace and applying shortcut-to-adiabaticity via inverse engineering, we design a robust protocol to achieve fast and high-fidelity state transfer in the cat-state qubit. We analyze the sensitivity to systematic control errors and identify an optimal robustness condition that strongly suppresses errors induced by imperfections in the driving fields. Furthermore, we show that dissipative confinement efficiently suppresses leakage out of the cat-state subspace caused by the pure dephasing, highlighting an intrinsic advantage of dissipative-cat qubits. This work establishes a robust and leakage-suppressing framework for high-fidelity bosonic qubit control, offering a promising route toward scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing.

item.title: Broadband Purcell Filter for Fast Superconducting Qubit Reset and Readout
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Purcell-limited relaxation time T1,P exceeds 1 ms over a 1.2 GHz bandwidth (4.7–5.9 GHz) with 500 ns readout and 100 ns reset at 99.6% efficiency. Dedicated reset resonator reduces photon-shot-noise dephasing sensitivity to γrst≈1.02 μs−1, a factor of 70 below the readout resonator.

Grade 0.462 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “circuit QED dispersive readout and Purcell-limited measurement” · Yu Zhao, Zhixu Chen, Hanxian Liu, Mingze Liu, Zixing Liu, Hao Pang, Meiyan Wan, Changkun Wu, Liuzhu Zhong, Sai Li, Yuefeng Yuan, Yuxuan Zhou, Ji Jiang, Ji Chu, Song Liu

Figure

Measured qubit relaxation time T1 and extracted Purcell limit T1,P plotted against qubit frequency, showing a Purcell-limited lifetime floor above 1 ms across 4.7 to 5.9 GHz alongside circuit model predictions.

Asks

Can a single Purcell filter architecture decouple fast reset and fast readout to allow independent optimization without degrading qubit coherence?

But

Demonstrated on a single transmon qubit Q1; requires 5 GHz high-pass filters on read-in/readout lines to suppress thermal photon occupation of the ∼4 GHz reset resonator.

Tools

flip-chip superconducting quantum processor · coplanar waveguide bandpass Purcell filter with two notches · dedicated low-frequency reset resonator · intentional κ-χ mismatch

Abstract

Rapid reset and readout of qubit states are essential for quantum error correction, yet accelerating these operations through stronger coupling to a dissipative environment inevitably increases qubit decay via the Purcell effect. Here we present a broadband Purcell filter that decouples the reset and readout paths, enabling both operations to be independently optimized without compromising qubit coherence. The filter employs two engineered notches - an intrinsic notch and a bandstop notch - to provide broadband Purcell protection, together with an additional reset stub that creates a reset mode below the protected band. To enable fast reset while suppressing filter-mediated interactions between qubits, we couple each qubit to a dedicated reset resonator. We experimentally demonstrate Purcell-limited relaxation times exceeding 1 ms across a 1.2 GHz bandwidth, simultaneously with 500 ns readout without a Josephson parametric amplifier and 100 ns reset with 99.6% efficiency. The reset resonator is designed with a deliberate kappa-chi mismatch, which suppresses photon-shot-noise-induced dephasing by a factor of 70 compared to the readout resonator. Our work provides a scalable hardware solution that resolves the traditional trade-off between fast qubit operations and qubit protection, advancing the prospects for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

item.title: Opto-Electrical Detection of Donor Bound Excitons in Silicon-on-Insulator Substrate
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Opto-electronic detection of donor bound excitons demonstrated in silicon-on-insulator devices. Transitions exhibit blue shifts of ∼100 μeV to ∼2 meV and linewidths broadened up to tenfold relative to bulk silicon.

Grade 0.456 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Silicon quantum electronics” · A. Kanniainen, A. S. Kumar, A. Sammak, G. Scappucci, J. T. Muhonen

Figure

Electrically detected photoconductivity response versus photon energy, showing resonance shifts and broadened donor bound exciton linewidths in SOI samples compared to bulk float-zone and Czochralski silicon.

Asks

Can donor-bound exciton transitions be detected opto-electrically in silicon-on-insulator substrates?

Before

All previous opto-electrical donor bound exciton measurements performed on bulk silicon.

But

Cryogenic temperature (T≈4 K), ensemble dopant measurements, magnetic fields below 400 mT.

Tools

Silicon-on-insulator (SOI) substrates · Isotopically enriched ²⁸Si device layers · Auger-mediated photoconductivity readout · Tunable diode laser (1045–1085 nm) · Pikus-Bir Hamiltonian strain modeling

Abstract

Spin of a donor bound electron in silicon has been shown to be a very coherent qubit system but lacks a coherent optical interface. There does, however, exist a donor bound exciton transition that can be excited optically but decays dominantly via an Auger recombination producing an electrical signal. This provides an opto-electrical pathway for spin readout. Scaling this readout to single-spin level will require interfacing the spins with silicon photonics for efficient guiding of photons, which in turn will require moving to silicon-on-insulator (SOI) substrates. Here we demonstrate first ensemble opto-electronic measurements of donor bound excitons in SOI material, including isotopically purified 28-Si device layers. The experiments show pronounced shifts in the resonance wavelengths and broadenings of the transition linewidths compared to the bulk experiments.

item.title: Probing Residual Noise at a Decoherence Sweet Spot in a ²⁸Si/SiGe Spin Qubit
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Operating a 28Si/SiGe spin qubit at a micromagnet decoherence-gradient sweet spot extends T2∗(31 s) to 67 μs (ergodic T2∗(∞)=35.6 μs) and CPMG coherence time to 4.6 ms, compared to T2∗(30 s)=5.2 μs at an adjacent dot 100 nm away.

Grade 0.456 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Silicon quantum electronics” · Shinwoo Lee (Seoul National University), Hanseo Sohn (Seoul National University), Jaemin Park (Seoul National University), Hyeongyu Jang (Seoul National University), Jonginn Yun (Seoul National University), Jun Yoneda (The University of Tokyo), Lucas E. A. Stehouwer (Delft University of Technology), Davide Degli Esposti (Delft University of Technology), Giordano Scappucci (Delft University of Technology), Dohun Kim (Seoul National University)

Figure

Ramsey fringes and decay curves showing T2∗=5.2 μs for the gradient-exposed qubit versus T2∗=67 μs at the sweet spot, alongside simulated stray-field profiles and CPMG coherence scaling with pulse number.

Asks

How far can inhomogeneous dephasing time T2∗ be extended in micromagnet-based 28Si/SiGe spin qubits by minimizing the longitudinal stray field gradient, and does residual 29Si nuclear spin noise limit coherence at that sweet spot?

Before

was a few microseconds to ~20 μs in micromagnet-based 28Si/SiGe devices even with 60 ppm 29Si enrichment

But

Residual charge noise persists locally via finite correlation with charge sensor (correlation strength up to 0.5 at 10−3–10−1 Hz); demonstrated on single sweet-spot dot rather than full array.

Tools

isotopically enriched ²⁸Si/SiGe quantum dot array (800 ppm ²⁹Si) · integrated Co micromagnet · electric-dipole spin resonance (EDSR) · CPMG dynamical decoupling · RF reflectometry charge sensing

Abstract

In ²⁸Si/SiGe spin qubits with micromagnets, the longitudinal stray field gradient transduces charge noise into qubit frequency noise and limits coherence. We compare two neighboring qubits in the same device with 800 ppm residual ²⁹Si, one near a decoherence sweet spot where the gradient is locally minimized and the other at a position with a larger gradient. At the sweet spot, T₂^* reaches 67 μs and the Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill coherence time reaches 4.6 ms, whereas T₂^* is 5.2 μs at the neighboring qubit. Near 1 Hz, the frequency noise power spectral density at the sweet spot is nearly two orders of magnitude lower than at the neighboring qubit. The magnitude and low-frequency decay of the residual spectrum are compatible with the prediction for ²⁹Si nuclear spin noise, and the weak interqubit correlation indicates that local noise becomes important for dephasing at the sweet spot. Despite a finite correlation with the charge sensor, sweet-spot operation strongly reduced the transduction of charge noise, bringing the residual frequency noise close to the level predicted for ²⁹Si nuclear spin fluctuations.

item.arxave:abstract: In ²⁸Si/SiGe spin qubits with micromagnets, the longitudinal stray field gradient transduces charge noise into qubit frequency noise and limits coherence. We compare two neighboring qubits in the same device with 800 ppm residual ²⁹Si, one near a decoherence sweet spot where the gradient is locally minimized and the other at a position with a larger gradient. At the sweet spot, T₂^* reaches 67 μs and the Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill coherence time reaches 4.6 ms, whereas T₂^* is 5.2 μs at the neighboring qubit. Near 1 Hz, the frequency noise power spectral density at the sweet spot is nearly two orders of magnitude lower than at the neighboring qubit. The magnitude and low-frequency decay of the residual spectrum are compatible with the prediction for ²⁹Si nuclear spin noise, and the weak interqubit correlation indicates that local noise becomes important for dephasing at the sweet spot. Despite a finite correlation with the charge sensor, sweet-spot operation strongly reduced the transduction of charge noise, bringing the residual frequency noise close to the level predicted for ²⁹Si nuclear spin fluctuations.
